title: What the falling number tells you
task: Match each reading to what it is evidence of.
scene: The wall shows the frequency dropping for eight seconds, then flattening out low. Aaron Whitlock has the log open. Two people have already named a cause.
assumes: the whole grid runs at one speed, and that speed is what frequency measures
takeaway: Frequency belongs to the whole system. Voltage belongs to one place.
why: Every generator on the grid turns in step, like a line of dancers. Frequency is the speed they are all turning at, so it is one number for the whole system. Take a generator away and the rest have to carry its share, which slows them all down together. How fast it falls says how big the gap is. Flattening out low is not recovery. It is the machines settling at a new, slower speed with the gap still there.

scenarios: Every substation reports the same frequency, to two decimal places.
It fell steeply for two seconds, and then more slowly.
The frequency has stopped falling, and is sitting below where it started.
Two substations report voltages three per cent apart.
choices: One number for the whole system, because every machine turns in step.
How big the gap is, against how much was spinning to absorb it.
A new balance at a slower speed, not the system getting better.
A local number, which is what makes it useful for saying where.
rebuttals: The same frequency everywhere is the machines turning in step, not a coincidence between meters.
How fast it fell measures the size of the gap. That is why it is the first thing to read.
Flattening out low is a new balance at a lower speed. It is not the system recovering.
Voltage is the local one. It says where, which is why it disagrees between substations.

title: How much went missing
task: Work out how much generation the system has lost.
scene: Haddad needs a number before starting anything. The demand has not moved. What has changed is how much the units still running can make between them.
assumes: the grid has to make exactly as much as it is using, every second
takeaway: The gap between what is needed and what is being made is the whole problem.
question: How much generation is missing?
why: A grid has to make exactly what it is using, second by second. There is no store. So when a unit trips, the gap is simply what was needed minus what is left. Here that is three hundred megawatts. The frequency falling is the machines already spinning giving up some of their speed to cover it, which they can do for seconds rather than minutes. That is the whole reason this is urgent.
answerText: Three hundred megawatts. That is what the system needs minus what is left running.

estimate.prompt: The system needs 6,400 megawatts. The units still running can make 6,100 between them.
estimate.question: How much generation is missing?
estimate.relationship: Missing = what is needed − what can be made.
estimate.explanation: The frequency figures describe what happened next. They are not the gap. The gap is a subtraction, and the two numbers for it are on the board.
labels: 0.30 Hz each second (how fast the frequency fell)

title: The order the records claim
task: Open what each record depends on, keep what stands, and name the bad clock.
scene: June Farrow has three records of the same eight seconds, and they disagree about what happened first. One was stamped by a clock nobody has checked since spring.
assumes: a timestamp is a measurement plus a clock, and either can be wrong
two records can agree because they share one clock
takeaway: Agreement only counts when the two things agreeing did not come from the same source.
question: Which records still support the order of events, and which clock explains the rest?
why: A timestamp is two things at once. Something that happened, and a clock saying when. Those fail separately. Two of these records were stamped by the same clock, so their agreement is one clock repeated, not two measurements. The recorder using satellite time has its own clock and kept the real order. The slow record cannot resolve fractions of a second, and it can still say which breakers opened.
answerText: Keep the satellite-timed recorder for the order, and the slow record for which breakers opened. The other two share the drifted clock, and that clock is the fault.

title: Act before the relay does
task: Set the thresholds before the trend is released.
scene: The line is carrying eight per cent more than it is rated for, and rising slowly. Novak wants a plan he can hand to the switching operator before the protection makes the choice for them.
assumes: a line has a steady limit and a short-term one, and they are different
moving generation about takes minutes, and shedding load is quick
takeaway: A rule has to fire early enough for the slow action to arrive in time.
question: At what loading should each action be committed, given how long each takes?
why: The short-term limit exists so somebody can decide, not so everybody can wait. The response comes in stages because the actions take different times. Moving generation about takes minutes, so it has to start while there is still room. Shedding load is quick, so it can wait for a higher number. Writing both down before the trend runs stops hindsight becoming policy. A sensible threshold that fires too late for its own action is still a failed rule.
answerText: Start moving generation at 110 per cent and shed load at 118. On this trend both then arrive before the ceiling at 120.

title: The power that never arrives
task: Work out how much of the power is lost as heat.
scene: Lindgren wants the loss figure before the morning call. The argument about moving generation about is really an argument about waste. The yard radio is still live beside them.
assumes: current pushing through a wire makes heat, and that heat is power that never arrives
takeaway: A wire warms up because some of the power is being spent on the wire itself.
question: How much of the power is being lost as heat?
why: Pushing current down a wire warms the wire, and that heat is power that never reaches anybody. About one and a half per cent of what this corridor carries is being spent that way. On eleven hundred and fifty megawatts that is seventeen, which is a small power station keeping the countryside warm. The share is not fixed either. Push more current down the same wire and the waste climbs faster than the current does.
answerText: About 17 megawatts, turned into warm air along the line.

estimate.prompt: The corridor is carrying 1,150 megawatts, and about 0.015 of that — one and a half per cent — is lost as heat in the wires.
estimate.question: How much of the power is being lost as heat?
estimate.relationship: Lost = what it carries × the share lost.
estimate.explanation: The share is written as a decimal already. Use one and a half instead of 0.015 and the answer comes out a hundred times too big.

title: What you are really protecting against
task: Say what makes the warm line worth acting on now.
scene: Reyes wants a decision. The line is inside its short-term limit for another half hour. The question on the table is what happens elsewhere if this one trips.
assumes: a network is supposed to survive losing any single line
takeaway: A limit only matters alongside what the flow does when that line is gone.
question: What makes the warm line a problem worth acting on now?
why: Running above the steady limit is a decision about time and heat, and the short-term limit exists so somebody can make it. What turns expensive into dangerous is what happens next. This line is already loaded. Lose it, and everything it was carrying lands on its neighbours, which were never sized for the sum. That second trip is protection working properly. Nobody chooses it.
answerText: Not the heat. If this line trips, its load lands on a neighbour that cannot take it, and that trip is nobody's decision.

choices: Being over the steady limit means damage starts at once.
If it trips, its flow lands on a neighbour that is not rated for it.
The seventeen megawatts of heat is enough to make the protection operate.
The protection has to trip before anybody can use the short-term limit.
rebuttals: The short-term limit exists precisely so a line can run above the steady one for a while. What follows a trip is the urgent part.
The heat is real, and it is not what the protection is watching for here.
The protection and the short-term limit are set to work together. The danger is the next line going over its own limit.

title: Why the far end sits low
task: Work out how big the drop is, as a share.
scene: The substation end of the feeder is at its proper voltage. Customers four kilometres out are complaining. The only meter is back at the substation.
assumes: current pushing along a wire uses up some of the voltage on the way
takeaway: A voltage measured at one end says nothing about the far end of a loaded line.
question: How big is the drop, as a share of what the feeder should be?
why: Voltage is the push, and pushing current down four kilometres of wire uses some of it up. So the far end always sits lower, and the busier the feeder the lower it goes. Here it drops about a tenth. That is enough for lights to dim and motors to labour, while the meter at the substation reads perfectly normal. The only way to know is to measure at the end.
answerText: About a tenth of what it should be — nearly ten per cent, all of it used up along the wire.

estimate.prompt: The far end sits about 1,070 volts below the substation. The feeder is supposed to run at 11,000 volts.
estimate.question: How big is the drop, as a share of what the feeder should be?
estimate.relationship: Share = the drop ÷ what it should be × 100.
estimate.explanation: Divide by the drop instead of into it and the answer is upside down. The current and the length explain why the drop is there, and neither is part of this sum.
labels: 4 km (how far out the customers are)

title: What actually limits a wire
task: Match each observation to the limit it is about.
scene: Novak has been asked to allow more current down a circuit for the afternoon. He wants each reason for saying no matched to the thing it is really about.
assumes: a wire warms up as current passes through it
takeaway: Current makes the heat. Voltage decides the spacing. They are separate limits.
why: Two different limits get muddled here. Heat comes from current, and it does not care what voltage the wire is at. The insulation and the gap to anything else care about voltage, and they do not care how much current is flowing. So a circuit can sit at exactly its right voltage and still be too hot. The drop at the far end is a third thing, and it is a customer's problem rather than a safety one.

scenarios: The wire is at 78 degrees, on a limit of 75.
The circuit has been switched to a higher voltage than it was built for.
Customers at the end report low voltage in the evening.
The span over the road has dropped a metre since morning.
choices: A heat limit, set by current and not by voltage at all.
An insulation limit, set by voltage and not by current.
A drop along the line, which is what current does over distance.
A clearance limit, and the one place where heat turns into safety.
rebuttals: Heating comes from the current, and it is the same whatever voltage the wire sits at.
Insulation and spacing are set by voltage, and they do not care how much current flows.
The drop comes from current along the line, and it reaches the customer before it reaches any limit.
Sag is the wire getting longer as it heats. It is the one place a heat limit becomes a clearance one.
columns: What it is a limit on

title: The order somebody will read back
task: Decide which circuit gets the first crew.
scene: Three crews, eleven dead feeders, and a list in front of Reyes that mixes household counts with a clinic and a pumping station. The phone is already ringing.
assumes: a crew can only work on one fault at a time
takeaway: The first crew goes where waiting costs most, not where the count is biggest.
question: Which feeder should take the first crew?
why: Two things decide this, and the number of households is only one. The first is what waiting costs. For a dialysis clinic that is treatments, not inconvenience. The second is how long the work takes. A one-hour job hands the crew back in time for another fault. The clinic circuit is worst on the first count and best on the second, so it goes first either way.
answerText: The clinic feeder. Waiting costs most there, and it is an hour's work, so the crew is free again for the next one.

choices: The feeder with 4,100 households, faulted at the substation, four hours' work.
The clinic feeder — 180 homes, one pole, an hour's work.
The feeder with 2,600 households and a fault nobody has found yet.
The feeder to the pumping station, which is running on its standby supply.
rebuttals: The biggest count is a four-hour job, and starting it ties a crew up for the whole shift.
A fault nobody has found cannot be given a time, so it cannot be lined up against the others.
The pumping station is running on standby. It is not off, and it can wait.

title: Power for four hours
task: Turn the power into the energy it delivered.
scene: Farrow has what the circuit was delivering on the night of the event, and how long it ran for. The report claims an energy figure nobody has been able to reproduce.
assumes: power says how fast energy is being delivered, and energy is what actually gets used
takeaway: Power is a rate. Energy is what the rate delivers over time, and the bill is in energy.
question: How much energy did the circuit deliver that night?
why: Power and energy get muddled constantly, and they are not the same thing. Power says how fast. Five and a half megawatts is a rate, like a tap running. Energy is what came out of the tap, and it depends on how long the tap was open. Four hours at 5.6 megawatts is 22.4 megawatt hours. It is the energy that gets billed, and the energy that runs out.
answerText: About 22.4 megawatt hours. That is the rate multiplied by the four hours it ran.

estimate.prompt: The circuit was delivering 5.6 megawatts, and it ran for four hours.
estimate.question: How much energy did it deliver?
estimate.explanation: The voltage and the current are how the power was worked out. Neither of them belongs in this sum, which is only about the rate and the hours.

title: Four things that have to agree
task: Put the steps of joining a machine to the grid in order.
scene: Haddad has a machine at rest and a grid running normally. She wants the order written down before anybody is standing at the panel with a hand on the switch.
assumes: a generator joined to a live grid is forced to turn at the grid's speed
takeaway: Every mismatch gets removed before the switch closes, and there is only one order that works.
why: Closing that switch ties the machine to the whole grid, and the grid does not adjust. So every difference has to go first. Speed first, because a machine turning at the wrong speed gets slammed into step, hard enough to damage it. Voltage next, or current pours between them for no useful reason. Then wait for the two waves to line up. Close them when all three match, and the machine simply joins in.

cards: Bring the machine up to the grid's speed.
Match its voltage to the grid's.
Wait until the two waves line up.

title: Two instruments, two numbers
task: Say how the two readings should relate if both are right.
scene: A scope on the busbar shows the voltage peaking at 325 volts. The panel meter beside it reads 230. Both were checked last month and neither has been touched.
assumes: an alternating voltage rises and falls, over and over, rather than sitting still
takeaway: An alternating voltage has no single value, so the number quoted has to say which one it is.
question: Which relation should hold if both instruments are right?
why: An alternating voltage is never one number. It rises to a peak, falls back through zero, and does the same the other way, fifty times a second. The scope shows the highest it reaches. The meter shows the steady voltage that would do the same work — heat the same kettle in the same time. For this shape of wave the peak sits about one and a half times higher, and 325 against 230 is exactly that. Two instruments, one voltage.
answerText: The peak is about 1.4 times the meter's reading. Both are right, and they are quoting different things about the same voltage.

choices: The peak is about 1.4 times the meter's number.
The peak is about twice the meter's number.
The meter's number is about 1.4 times the peak.
The meter's number is about half the peak.
rebuttals: Twice would make the peak 460, and the scope is showing 325.
The meter reads lower than the peak, so multiplying it the other way goes in the wrong direction.
Half of 325 is about 163, which is not what the meter is showing.

title: What comes out against what went in
task: Work out what share of the stored energy comes back.
scene: The battery charged overnight on Saturday and gave it back into Sunday's peak. Alvarez has both totals and the brochure figure, and the three do not agree.
assumes: putting energy into a store and taking it out again both waste some of it
takeaway: What a store is worth is the share that comes back, not the size on the label.
question: What share of the energy put in comes back out?
why: Nothing stores energy for free. Some is lost going in, some coming out, and some keeping the thing cool while it sits there. So the number that matters is simply what came out divided by what went in. Here that is 187 out of 220, which is about eighty-five per cent. Fifteen per cent of everything that went in never came back. The power rating on the label is a different claim. It says how fast, not how much.
answerText: About 85 per cent. Fifteen per cent of everything put in never comes back out.

estimate.prompt: The store took in 220 megawatt hours overnight, and gave back 187 into Sunday's peak.
estimate.question: What share of the energy put in comes back out?
estimate.explanation: The rating and the hours describe how the store behaves. Multiply them together and you get a number that has nothing to do with this question.
labels: 4 h (how long it can run for)

title: Why the wires are not at wall voltage
task: Say what raising the voltage does to the current and the waste.
scene: A visitor asks Haddad why the machine makes power at twenty thousand volts and the line outside runs at four hundred thousand.
assumes: for the same power, a higher voltage means less current
takeaway: The same power can be delivered in more than one way, and the ways waste very different amounts.
question: For the same power, what happens when the voltage is raised twenty times?
why: Power is the push multiplied by the flow. So for the same power, a bigger push needs less flow. Raise the voltage twenty times and the current falls to a twentieth. The waste in the wires depends on the current twice over, so a twentieth of the current wastes four hundred times less. That is why long lines run at enormous voltages. The insulation is harder and more expensive, and the saving is far bigger.
answerText: The current falls twenty times, and the waste in the wires falls four hundred times, because it depends on the current twice over.

choices: The current falls twenty times, and the waste falls four hundred times.
The current falls twenty times, and the waste falls twenty times.
The current stays the same, and only the insulation changes.
The current rises twenty times, and the waste rises four hundred times.
rebuttals: For the same power, current falls as voltage rises. The waste then falls faster still, because it depends on the current twice over.
The insulation does get harder, and the reason for doing it is the enormous drop in current and waste.
Raising the voltage for the same power lowers the current. It does not raise it.

title: What is worth knowing before the peak
task: Spend the budget on what could change tonight's decision.
scene: Reyes has a small budget and four things she could find out before the evening peak. Only some of them would change what she does about the reserve.
assumes: reserve is held against what nobody knows, rather than against the forecast itself
takeaway: A measurement is worth buying when its answer could still change what you do.
question: Which measurements are worth buying before six o'clock?
why: Reserve is held against two things. How wrong the demand forecast could be, and whether the things being counted on can actually deliver. Measuring how this winter's cold has been driving demand narrows the first. Testing the store at the rate it would really be called on settles the second. Repeating a generator test that is already valid buys reassurance. A survey that lands in six weeks cannot change tonight, however good it is.
answerText: Buy this winter's cold-and-demand figures, and the store tested at the rate it would really be used. Both can still change tonight.

title: What a short circuit is limited by
task: Work out the current the fault drew.
scene: The cable failed and shorted to earth. The push behind it is 6,350 volts, and the whole path back to the source resists 0.42 ohms. Novak wants the current the switchgear had to break.
assumes: a short circuit is a path with almost nothing in the way
takeaway: A fault current is set by the path back to the source, and by nothing else.
question: How much current flowed during the fault?
why: Normally the current is set by whatever is drawing power at the far end. A short circuit goes round all of that. So the only things left holding it back are the wire and the machinery behind it. Push divided by resistance is fifteen thousand amps, about fifty times the normal load. That is why switchgear has its own rating for breaking a fault.
answerText: About fifteen thousand amps — roughly fifty times the normal load, because the fault goes around everything that usually limits it.

estimate.prompt: The push at the fault is 6,350 volts, and the whole path back to the source resists 0.42 ohms.
estimate.question: How much current flowed during the fault?
estimate.relationship: Current = the push ÷ what resists it.
estimate.explanation: The normal load does not limit a fault, because the fault has gone round it. The clearing time decides how much damage it does, not how big it gets.
labels: 0.08 s (how long it took to clear)

title: A reading with no connection
task: Change one thing at a time, and find what makes the signal appear.
scene: June Farrow has a safe low-voltage test rig beside the yard diagram. It shows the current going in, the signal coming out, and a core she can open. She wants a cause rather than a definition.
assumes: a changing magnetic field can make a voltage appear in a nearby coil
takeaway: What makes a signal appear here is change. A steady current makes a field and no signal.
question: Which change makes the signal disappear, and does it come back when you undo it?
why: There is no wire between the two sides of this device. What crosses is a magnetic field, made by the current going in. A field on its own does nothing to the coil. It has to be changing. Alternating current changes direction fifty times a second, so a signal appears. Steady current makes a steady field and nothing else.
answerText: The kind of current. Alternating gives about 5 amps out. Steady drops it to nearly nothing, and switching back brings it straight to 5.

title: Isolated is not yet safe
task: Say what has to happen before the crew touches the conductor.
scene: The cable is cut off at both ends and a tester reads dead at the work point. Kowalczyk stops the crew, because one step is still missing. There is live equipment nearby.
assumes: a conductor can be brought back to life from more than one direction
takeaway: Isolating and testing say what is true now. Earthing keeps it true.
question: What has to happen after isolating and testing dead?
why: Isolating and testing answer different questions, and neither answers the one that matters. Opening both ends removes the sources anybody knows about. The tester says it is dead now. Neither promises it stays dead if somebody switches something. Earthing gives any surprise somewhere easy to go, instead of through a person. It turns a fact into a condition.
answerText: Earth it at the point of work. Isolating and testing say it is dead now. Earthing is what keeps it dead if something changes.

choices: Earth the conductor at the point of work.
Repeat the dead test every five minutes while they work.
Leave it unearthed, so any surprise voltage still shows on a tester.
Close a switch briefly, to prove the protection would trip.
rebuttals: Repeating the test is a series of snapshots. An earth makes a surprise survivable rather than merely visible.
An unearthed conductor can be pushed to a dangerous voltage by the lines beside it.
Deliberately putting power back into the work area is not a test. The order is isolate, prove dead, earth.

title: The peak, and what the cold adds
task: Work out tomorrow's evening peak.
scene: A normal Friday this week of the year peaks at 6,400 megawatts. Lindgren's own figure for this winter is 120 megawatts more for every degree below zero. Tomorrow is minus four.
assumes: demand goes up as the temperature goes down, roughly in step
takeaway: A forecast is a normal shape plus what the weather adds, and the second part gets measured.
question: What should tomorrow's evening peak be?
why: Demand looks much the same most days, because people do much the same things at much the same times. What moves it is weather. The useful way to hold that is a figure for what one degree is worth on this system, measured from this winter rather than taken from a book. Here it is a hundred and twenty megawatts a degree, and tomorrow is four degrees below. So the peak lands near six thousand nine hundred.
answerText: About 6,880 megawatts. That is the normal Friday peak plus four degrees of cold at 120 megawatts each.

estimate.prompt: A normal Friday peaks at 6,400 megawatts. This winter, demand rises 120 megawatts for every degree below zero. Tomorrow is four degrees below.
estimate.question: What should tomorrow's evening peak be?
estimate.relationship: Peak = the normal peak + what one degree adds × how many degrees below zero.
estimate.explanation: The reserve covers how wrong this could be. It is a separate decision, and adding it here counts the same worry twice.

title: Cheapest first, and the exceptions
task: Match each plant to why it sits where it does.
scene: Four plants and an order to sign. Reyes wants each one matched to the real reason it sits where it does, rather than to its price.
assumes: generators are normally run cheapest first
takeaway: Cheapest first is the rule, and three things bend it: where a plant is, how fast it moves, and whether it can be relied on.
why: Running the cheapest first is what keeps electricity affordable. Three things bend that order. A plant that costs almost nothing to run goes first, and if nobody can promise its output, something reliable stays behind it. A plant that can change output fast is worth holding at half, because the other half is what gets called on. And a plant in the right place can be needed whatever it costs.

scenarios: The ridge fleet, almost free to run, with output nobody can promise.
A gas machine that can move fast, deliberately left at half output.
An old station on the wrong side of the line, kept off despite a middling price.
An old station on the right side of a bottleneck, run despite being dear.
choices: First in the queue on cost, with something reliable kept behind it.
Held at half output on purpose, because only a half-loaded machine has spare.
Kept off, because running it would push flow onto a line that cannot take it.
Run out of turn because of where it is, not what it costs.
rebuttals: Costing nothing to run puts it first, and output nobody can promise is why something reliable stays behind it.
Holding a fast machine at half output is buying spare. A machine at full output has none to sell.
Being in the right place can be worth more than being cheap, when the cheap one overloads a line.
Dear and slow means last. It is the plant the system is trying not to need.
columns: Why it sits where it does

title: When the cheapest power cannot get out
task: Decide what to do with more wind than the line can carry.
scene: Sarraf can make 340 megawatts on the ridge tonight. The line out of the valley carries about 190. There is no second way out.
assumes: power has to have a path to wherever it is used
takeaway: Electricity that cannot reach anybody is not electricity, whatever it cost to make.
why: A line at its limit is a wall, not a preference, so some of tonight's wind is not going anywhere. The only question is what the system buys instead. A second line fixes it for good and takes years. A store on the ridge moves the surplus in time rather than in space, which is the right shape for a problem that happens forty nights a winter. Paying the fleet to stop is what happens meanwhile, and it buys nothing.
answerText: Some of it has to stop, and the useful move is a store on the ridge. It shifts tonight's surplus into hours when the line is free.

title: What the dark hours cost
task: Turn the lost power into the energy nobody got.
scene: The valley was drawing about 300 megawatts when it went dark. Haddad expects two and a half hours to bring it back, and the report wants energy rather than power.
assumes: power kept up over a stretch of time delivers energy
takeaway: Power is the rate. Energy is the amount, and everything is settled in energy.
question: How much energy did the valley never get?
why: Power says how fast electricity is arriving. Energy says how much arrived. Both get called demand, which is why they get muddled. Multiply the power by the hours it was missing and you get energy: three hundred megawatts for two and a half hours is seven hundred and fifty megawatt hours. That is the figure every claim and every inquiry runs on, because it grows with the length of the outage.
answerText: About 750 megawatt hours never delivered. Three hundred megawatts, for two and a half hours.

estimate.prompt: The valley was drawing about 300 megawatts when it collapsed. Bringing it back is expected to take two and a half hours.
estimate.question: How much energy did the valley never get?
estimate.relationship: Energy = power × the time it was missing.
estimate.explanation: The number of households and the frequency both matter to the story, and neither belongs in this sum. One is who it happened to. The other is why.
labels: 2.5 h (how long to bring it back)

title: The order physics allows
task: Build the restart path, then name the link that decides it.
scene: One hydro machine that can start with no outside power. A dead network. And a room that wants the big station back first. Nothing gets switched until the order is written down.
assumes: the big station needs electricity for its own pumps and fans before it can start
the hydro machine can start with no supply at all
takeaway: The biggest machine is useless until something smaller can wake it up.
question: How does starting power reach the big station, and which link decides it?
why: A dead network cannot start from its biggest generator, because that machine needs power before it can make any. Pumps, fans, controls. The hydro machine is different: water pushes the turbine round with no electricity involved at all. So it goes first, and its output travels down a small feeder to wake the big station's own equipment. That small feeder is the link everything waits on. It only has to carry the auxiliaries.
answerText: Water, hydro turbine, hydro generator, small feeder, the big station's own pumps and fans, then the big generator. The small feeder decides it.

title: Why it cannot go faster
task: Match each step of the restart to what limits it.
scene: Obi has crews asking why the restart is moving a few streets at a time. The substation is live and the whole feeder could be closed in one movement.
assumes: a small live system is upset far more by a given block of load than a big one
takeaway: Every step is limited by something different, and rushing the wrong one collapses it again.
why: What limits the restart changes as it grows. Very early, the live piece is tiny, so any block of load is enormous next to it and the frequency dives. Long lines with almost nothing on them push the voltage up rather than down, which is the opposite of most people's instinct. Streets that have been off in winter come back higher than normal, because every heater is calling at once. And joining two live systems is a matching problem.

scenarios: Adding the first blocks of load to a very small live island.
Energising a long line with almost nothing on it.
Restoring a street that has been off for two hours in winter.
Joining the restored island back to its neighbour.
choices: A frequency limit, because a small system cannot take a big step.
A voltage limit, because a lightly loaded line pushes the far end up.
A cold-load limit, because everything that was off comes back at once.
A matching limit, because both sides have to agree before the switch closes.
rebuttals: Early on the island is small, so any block is a large share of it. That is a frequency limit.
A long line with little on it pushes the voltage up rather than down, which is a voltage limit.
Cold load comes back above normal, because every heater in the street is calling at once.
Joining two live systems is about matching them, not about how much either can carry.

title: Which of the three cannot wait
task: Keep the one that cannot wait, and hand the rest over properly.
scene: Reyes has three live problems on the board and can only keep one herself. Whitlock is ready to take a handover, and she will not accept an instruction that amounts to watch it.
assumes: a bad problem that is not getting worse is different from a small one that is
getting reserve in place takes time before the peak
takeaway: Urgency is about how fast something is getting worse and whether somebody else can own the next move.
question: What do you keep, and what exactly do you hand over?
why: The cable fault is loud and stable. Those customers are already off, and a crew is on the way. The machine running out of fuel has a known time and a known size, so somebody else can line up its replacement. The forecast error is different. It is still growing, and getting reserve in place takes hours. Every update that goes by without a decision removes choices nobody can get back.
answerText: Keep the forecast error, because it is still growing. Hand the cable fault to the field team and the fuel-limited machine to the generation desk. Each gets a first move and a number.

title: The same line, busier
task: Work out what the line is wasting now.
scene: With the feeder out, the flow has shifted and the line is carrying more than it was. Novak wants the heat figure before deciding whether the evening needs a switching change.
assumes: the busier a wire is, the larger the share of the power it turns into heat
takeaway: When something counts twice over, a small rise in it is a big rise in the result.
question: How much is the line wasting as heat now?
why: An hour ago this line carried eleven hundred and fifty megawatts and wasted about seventeen. Now it carries twelve hundred and eighty and wastes about twenty. The flow went up about a ninth. The waste went up about a fifth. That is because the heat depends on the current twice over, so it always outruns the flow. And the limit on the line is a heat limit, so the margin disappears faster than the loading suggests.
answerText: About 20 megawatts, against 17 an hour ago. The flow rose about a ninth and the waste rose about a fifth.

estimate.prompt: The line now carries 1,280 megawatts, and about 0.016 of that — one and six tenths per cent — is lost as heat.
estimate.question: How much is the line wasting as heat now?
estimate.relationship: Lost = what it carries × the share lost.
estimate.explanation: The share itself has gone up, from 0.015 to 0.016, because a busier wire wastes a bigger fraction. That is why the answer rises faster than the flow.
labels: 1,150 MW (what it carried an hour ago)

title: An order that survives being carried out
task: Put the evening's four moves in order.
scene: Lindgren has four moves for the evening and no view on the order. Two of them change what the others are worth, and one cannot be undone inside the shift.
assumes: some actions change what the actions after them are worth
takeaway: Do what improves your information first, and what you cannot undo last.
why: Fix the forecast first, because every other number is sized against it. Get that wrong and you do the right thing in the wrong amount. Bring the reserve forward next. It costs money rather than customers, and it can be handed back. Then start loading the replacement plant, which needs real minutes and has to be underway before the fuel runs down. Reconfiguring the network goes last, because it is the one nobody can quietly undo.

cards: Fix the forecast, so every other number is sized against something real.
Bring the reserve forward, to cover the machine coming off at six.
Start loading the replacement plant, which needs the minutes.
Reconfigure the network around the faulted feeder.

title: Measured, worked out, or suspected
task: Spend the two checks on the claims that need them.
scene: June Farrow has four statements ready for the final report and two checks left before it is signed. Some are already backed. Others are still a suspicion.
assumes: a claim can be measured, worked out, or still only suspected
there is not enough time to check everything
takeaway: A signature is only worth the evidence behind it, so check the important claims that have none.
question: Which claims deserve the two checks before they become findings?
why: The four claims are not equally supported. The sensor being wrong has been shown two separate ways, with a date to match, so it is settled. The wire having lost strength is good reasoning and nobody has tested a piece of it. The store's efficiency is measured, and it is not what the inquiry turns on. The relay explanation is both central and unproved. Two checks, and they belong on the claims that matter and have nothing under them.
answerText: Check the wire's strength and the relay explanation. The sensor is already backed two ways, and the store's efficiency is not what the inquiry turns on.

title: The number that has to be a range
task: Say why the winter peak goes in as a range.
scene: Lindgren's winter peak goes into the report. He wants the width written into the sentence, and Reyes wants to know what the width is for.
assumes: a forecast covers a spread of outcomes, not just one
takeaway: A prediction is only usable by a planner if it says how wrong it might be.
question: Why does the winter peak go in as a range rather than one figure?
why: Reserve is not held against the peak everybody expects. It is held against how far above that the peak might land, which is a fact about the width and not about the middle. Print a single number and the one quantity a planner needs has been deleted, so the planner invents one, usually too small. The width is also the honest part of the forecast. It says which conditions the model was built on and which it has never seen.
answerText: Because reserve is sized against how far above the middle the peak might land. That is the width, and a single number deletes it.

choices: Because reserve has to cover how far above the middle the peak could land.
Because a range stops one odd winter counting as the model being wrong.
Because the middle cannot be measured until winter is over, and the width can.
Because a range already includes the reserve the operators have scheduled.
rebuttals: A range makes the forecast easier to test, not harder. A peak outside it counts against the model.
Both the middle and the width are worked out before the season. Neither waits for the actual peak.
The forecast and the reserve are separate decisions. The width informs the reserve; it does not contain it.

title: What outlives the emergency
task: Say which of the fortnight's changes should stay.
scene: Four things the room started doing under pressure. Reyes asks which are worth their cost on an ordinary Monday, when nothing at all is going wrong.
assumes: a habit taken up in an emergency has a cost that only shows later
takeaway: Keep what would have caught it early. Drop what only paid off because the fortnight was strange.
question: Which of the fortnight's changes is most worth keeping?
why: One of these would have caught the whole thing. The sensor was wrong for months, because nothing was ever compared against it. Comparing it costs an afternoon. Extra reserve costs money every night for a benefit on a few of them. Reading the loading four times as often would have changed nothing at all. Those readings were wrong, rather than late.
answerText: Cross-check any instrument a decision rests on against something independent. That is the one that would have caught this months earlier.

choices: Cross-check any instrument a decision rests on, against something independent.
Hold the extra reserve at the fortnight's level all winter.
Report line loading every fifteen minutes instead of every hour.
Require two operators to sign any load shedding.
rebuttals: Extra reserve costs money every night for a benefit on a few nights. That is a question about the forecast width.
The loading readings were wrong, not late. Reporting a wrong number four times as often adds nothing.
A second signature slows down the one decision that was both right and urgent.
